chunks: Flying probe testing. The question: What is flying probe testing? What can it capture?
Flying probe testing does the same electrical check as in-circuit test: it finds shorts, broken connections and wrong or missing parts. But it needs no custom fixture.
A few motorized probes, typically four to eight, move over the board, touch a pad, take a measurement, lift and move on. The program comes from the design data (the netlist).
It is slow per board, but it has almost no setup cost.
Think of a bed of nails pressing hundreds of pins at once, compared with a single person tapping spots with a few fingers, one after another.
The fingers can reach any spot with no special tooling, so changing the board design costs little. But tapping spot after spot takes much longer than one big press.
The choice depends on how many boards you must test.
Four probe heads, two above and two below the board, each running on a rail and moving in X/Y (and plunging in Z). Each head touches one point (orange) at a time.
A measurement uses two or more probes at once: one drives, one senses, and others guard.
Flying probe: a few moving test probes on motorized arms, with no fixture. Netlist: the list of which pins connect to which, taken from the design data.
Test point or pad: a spot the probe can touch to reach a net. Step: one probe move plus one measurement. Fixture: a custom holder of many pins for one board design.
Say a board needs 2,000 steps, and each step takes 0. 1 seconds. That is 2,000 x 0. 1 = 200 seconds, about 3. 3 minutes per board. A fixture-based tester might take 30 seconds.
But the fixture can cost thousands of USD, and the flying probe only needs a program.
The page's cost example assumes a slower 8-minute flying probe test: 800 USD to program and about 5. 33 USD of machine time per board, against a 9,000 USD fixture at about 0.
50 USD per board. Then the fixture becomes cheaper above roughly 1,700 boards. Below that, the flying probe wins. That is the whole idea.

"Flying probe test checks a board without a custom fixture: a few motorised probes touch down on pads, vias and leads one after another and measure opens, shorts and component values, programmed straight from CAD.
It's flexible, so great for prototypes, low volume and changing designs, and can reach fine features on both sides.
But it takes minutes per board and can't test at speed or check real function, so above some volume, around 1,700 boards in a typical cost example, a bed-of-nails fixture is cheaper."
